newsitem.title: JORDAN: Funds buying Jordan shares, hope for 1997 reforms.
newsitem.headline: Funds buying Jordan shares, hope for 1997 reforms.

text.p: Foreign buying in Jordan's stock exchange has picked up sharply in the last two months in anticipation of a government drive to speed up economic reforms in 1997, Jordanian financial analysts said on Monday.
Jordanian investment managers said they saw growing signs since December of dedicated Middle East funds, which include Jordan as a main component, and global funds picking up blue-chip shares.

"At least 10 established Middle East funds have entered the market and built up portfolios over the last two months," said Zaid al-Basha, securities manager at Jordan's British Bank of the Middle East.

Analysts estimate over the last two months global funds have accounted for around $11 million, or 16 percent, of a total $70 million trading turnover on the Amman exchange. That compares with $21 million for the whole of last year.
Funds focused on a dozen bluechip industrials and banks including mainly state-owned potash, phosphates and cement and a handful of leading drug and tourism firms.

Omar Masri, managing director of Atlas Investment Group, while not expecting a major inflow in first quarter 1997, said Middle East specialist funds which follow the market on a daily basis are "seeking to position themselves selectively in anticipation of a rebound."

He said the funds would be closely watching for progress in Jordan's IMF-directed economic reforms before stepping up their purchases. Rapid reforms and state sell-offs in other regional markets like Egypt, and Arab company listings outside the region have helped eclipse Jordan's bourse in 1996.

Global fund managers complain of a shortage of available shares in the popular bluechip firms due to both a 50 percent foreign ownership ceiling and local investors holding on to stock bought at high prices, further hindering supply.
They estimate less than five percent is available in bluechips, since most are either majority government-owned or already near the ceiling.
A new company law that abolishes a 15 percent tax on capitalisation, due to be approved this month by Parliament, should add more freefloating bluechip shares.
Arab Bank, Islamic Bank, Jordan Investment Finance Bank and Industrial Development Bank all plan to distribute bonus shares once the companies law is enacted.

Another major breathrough will be a new securities law that overhauls the bourses structure and its regulatory framework to allow for the setting up of mutual funds, Global Depository Receipts and corporate bonds -- all non existent now.

Brokers say a key test will be how far the government goes in 1997 to start implementing a pledge to sell off government owned shares -- estimated to be around 35 percent of the market's capitalisation -- to add market depth.

Global funds' stake on the bourse is just 1.5 percent of a total market capitalisation of 3.5 billion dinars against a 33 percent held by non-Jordanian Arab investors. The rest is held by the government and Jordanian investors.
Investment analysts say lifting a 50 percent ceiling in foreign ownership which a government committee is currently examing would raise Jordan's profile in the region.
